strengths: Introduces a clean and well-motivated theoretical framework (evaluability, weak vs. strong evaluability) that formalizes an important and underexplored question: when can a performance metric for generative models be reliably assessed from finite held-out samples, as opposed to merely estimated?

Provides a fairly comprehensive taxonomy of results across a wide range of commonly used metrics: IPMs (with VC-dimension and fat-shattering-dimension dichotomies), fixed statistical tests, α-Rényi/KL divergence, the coverage profile, TV distance, and perplexity/NLL, giving the paper broad scope and internal coherence (nicely summarized in Table 1).

The extension of Bousquet et al. (2019)'s factor-3 optimality result from TV distance to general binary-valued IPM classes (Theorem 3.2) is a meaningful and non-trivial generalization, and the negative result that no finite taxonomy of sample complexities exists for estimable IPMs (Theorem 3.6) is an interesting, somewhat surprising structural finding.

The negative results for Rényi/KL divergence and the coverage profile give a rigorous theoretical explanation for well-documented empirical phenomena (e.g., perplexity's poor correlation with downstream task performance), connecting theory to practically observed issues in LLM evaluation.

Proofs (checked in the appendix) use standard but correctly applied tools (Hoeffding/Chernoff bounds, Hellinger–TV relations, VC/fat-shattering uniform convergence) and the constructions used for impossibility results (e.g., rare-event constructions for Rényi/KL, near-threshold constructions for coverage profile) are intuitive and clearly explained.

The discussion sections (e.g., on why perplexity/NLL is geometrically misaligned with bounded, rare-event-tolerant metrics) provide useful conceptual takeaways beyond the formal theorems, and the paper is honest about open questions (e.g., optimality of the factor-3 bound for real-valued IPMs, relationship between strong evaluability and estimability).
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical illustration or validation; given that several conclusions are motivated by observed failures of perplexity in practice, even small-scale simulations or synthetic experiments (e.g., replicating the constructions in Theorems 4.2/5.3 numerically) would substantially strengthen the connection between theory and practice and help readers calibrate how severe these issues are at realistic sample sizes.

The positive/constructive results largely rely on somewhat ad hoc auxiliary assumptions (Δ-closeness in ratio, (N,α)-margin, lower-bound support Assumption 4.6) introduced specifically to rescue evaluability for particular metrics; the paper does not clearly argue these assumptions are realistic or verifiable in practice, leaving the practical guidance for practitioners underdeveloped relative to the largely negative theoretical picture.

Some central results build closely on prior work (Bousquet et al. 2019, Yatracos 1985, Alon et al. 1997) via natural generalizations, and a few key claims are left open (e.g., optimality of the 3-factor for real-valued IPMs in Proposition 3.4, whether strong evaluability implies estimability), somewhat limiting the completeness of the 'nearly complete characterization' claimed in the contributions.

The definition of evaluability itself (pairwise ranking comparison up to multiplicative/additive slack) is a reasonable but specific choice, and the paper does not thoroughly justify why this particular notion (rather than, e.g., regret-based or top-k selection notions) is the most appropriate formalization of 'can generative models be evaluated statistically,' nor does it explore alternative definitions.

The coverage profile relies on a very recent (2025) arXiv preprint as its primary motivation/justification, and the practical significance of this specific metric relative to other truncated-divergence proposals in the literature (e.g., ε-perplexity, Pillutla et al. 2021) is not deeply engaged with, despite being highlighted as a main contribution area.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy throughout; while the introduction provides good intuition, subsequent sections would benefit from more worked examples or diagrams to make the results (especially the dichotomies and margin conditions) more accessible to readers not deeply versed in statistical learning theory.

strengths: The paper introduces a clean formal vocabulary (estimability, strong/weak evaluability) that cleanly separates the question of whether a metric can be point-estimated from whether it can at least be used to correctly rank two models, which is a useful conceptual distinction not previously made explicit in this generality.

The dichotomy results for IPMs (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.4) connecting evaluability to VC dimension and fat-shattering dimension are mathematically clean and give an interpretable picture of when test-based metrics can or cannot be reliably compared from finite samples.

The negative results for Rényi/KL divergence and the coverage profile (Theorems 4.2, Proposition 4.5) are intuitive and the constructions, while simple, convincingly illustrate how rare, low-probability support points can make these metrics statistically untestable, which is a point of genuine conceptual interest for the community studying LLM evaluation.

The treatment of perplexity/NLL as a score function (Section 5), including the positive result under a ratio-closeness assumption (Proposition 5.5) and negative result for restricted KL (Theorem 5.3), nicely operationalizes an informal, widely discussed empirical observation (that perplexity doesn't correlate with downstream quality) into a formal statement.
Results are self-contained with full proofs provided in the appendix, aiding verifiability of claims within the stated framework.
weaknesses: The evaluability definition (Def. 2.3) quantifies the score function after fixing the pair of models (q1, q2): 'for any two models q1, q2 ... there exists ... a score function s'. This permits the scoring rule to be tailored/aware of the specific candidate pair being compared (as is explicitly used in the proof of Theorem 3.2, which relies on Bousquet et al.'s density-estimation algorithm that takes the candidate class {q1, q2} as input). This is a materially weaker and less practically relevant notion than a single fixed scoring rule (e.g., perplexity) that must correctly rank *any* pair of models it is applied to, which is how such metrics are actually used in practice. The paper does not clearly flag or discuss this subtlety, which could make several of the 'positive' 3-weak-evaluability results less meaningful than they appear.

The work is purely theoretical with no empirical validation or illustrative experiments connecting the abstract impossibility/possibility results to actual generative model evaluation (e.g., real language models, real benchmarks). Claims in the introduction and discussion that the theory 'explains' observed empirical phenomena (perplexity's poor correlation with downstream performance) are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Several central results are incomplete: Proposition 3.4 (real-valued IPM dichotomy) explicitly lacks a matching lower bound establishing that factor 3 is optimal, and multiple major results are reduced to open questions in Section 6 (strict dichotomy for real-valued IPMs, relationship between estimability and strong evaluability, evaluability of β-restricted KL beyond the NLL score). This leaves the paper's main technical narrative only partially resolved.

The core technical machinery for the binary IPM dichotomy (Theorem 3.2) is a relatively direct reduction to/adaptation of existing density-estimation results from Bousquet et al. (2019) and Yatracos (1985); the novelty here is largely reframing rather than new proof technique, somewhat limiting the originality of the strongest result in the paper.

The negative-result constructions throughout (Theorems 4.2, 5.3, Proposition 4.5) rely on extreme, low-dimensional (2-3 point), vanishingly small probability mass examples. While mathematically valid for establishing impossibility, the paper does not discuss how such worst-case constructions relate to realistic structured domains (e.g., natural language) where additional regularity might restore practical evaluability, leaving the practical implications somewhat overstated relative to what is proven.

The paper's significance for the ICML audience is unclear beyond a niche theoretical contribution: it offers limited actionable guidance for practitioners (e.g., it does not propose or validate alternative evaluation metrics/procedures that are both evaluable and practically informative), and the 'open questions' heavy ending suggests the work is preliminary rather than a complete, polished contribution.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean and novel distinction between 'estimability' (approximating a metric's value) and 'evaluability' (correctly ranking two models), which is a meaningful reframing of the classical question of when population quantities can be learned from samples, specifically tailored to the practical use case of comparing generative models.

Provides a fairly comprehensive and technically rigorous set of results across several metric families: a near-complete dichotomy for IPMs (VC dimension for binary tests, fat-shattering dimension for real-valued tests), negative results for Rényi/KL divergences and the coverage profile, and a careful dissection of when perplexity/NLL can or cannot serve as a valid scoring rule for TV distance and restricted KL divergence.

The results are generally well motivated with clean constructions (e.g., the rare-event construction used repeatedly to show non-evaluability of Rényi/KL divergences and coverage profile) that clearly illustrate the underlying mechanism (rare, unobserved events driving divergence values).

The paper is self-aware about its own limitations, explicitly listing open questions (e.g., whether a strict 3-factor dichotomy holds for real-valued IPMs, whether strong evaluability implies estimability, evaluability of β-restricted KL beyond NLL), which is a positive sign of honest scholarship.

The discussion connecting the theoretical findings to a well-known empirical puzzle (perplexity's poor correlation with downstream task performance) gives the theory some applied resonance, and the Assumption 5.4 margin condition for recovering NLL's usefulness is a nice, interpretable positive result.
weaknesses: The formal definition of evaluability (Definition 2.3) allows the score function s (and the sample-complexity function m) to depend on the specific pair of models q1, q2 being compared, rather than requiring a single fixed scoring rule that works uniformly across all models. This is a considerably weaker and less practically meaningful notion than what is typically needed in practice (a single evaluation score used to rank many systems), and the paper does not sufficiently discuss or justify this choice, nor characterize how much of the positive results would survive under a pair-independent (uniform) score function requirement.

The work is entirely theoretical with no empirical illustration or simulation, even on toy/synthetic settings, to validate or make tangible the practical relevance of the evaluability/non-evaluability distinctions (e.g., demonstrating the constructed adversarial distributions numerically, or showing perplexity's instability on a concrete example). This weakens the paper's connection to the motivating empirical phenomena it cites (e.g., perplexity's poor correlation with downstream performance).

The connection to the substantial existing literature on distribution property estimation and testing (e.g., sample complexity of estimating KL/Rényi divergence, entropy, and other symmetric functionals without full support knowledge) is largely missing; several of the qualitative conclusions (rare events make divergence estimation hard without additional structure) echo known results in that literature, and the paper would benefit from clarifying what is genuinely new relative to this body of work.

Some of the main results and proof techniques closely mirror or directly extend prior work (Bousquet et al. 2019, Yatracos 1985, Alon et al. 1997), and the degree of technical novelty beyond adapting known uniform-convergence/density-estimation machinery to the new evaluability definitions could be more clearly delineated.

The practical computability of the proposed strongly-evaluable score functions (e.g., dF(q, q̂) for IPMs, or density estimation procedures) is not discussed; these can be computationally expensive or require explicit knowledge of the test class F, which may limit real-world applicability even where the metric is theoretically evaluable.

The treatment of the coverage profile and restricted KL divergence, while interesting, relies on fairly strong and somewhat artificial margin/closeness assumptions (Assumptions 4.7 and 5.4) whose plausibility in realistic generative modeling scenarios (e.g., LLMs with huge discrete vocabularies) is not discussed or justified.

strengths: Introduces a clean and well-motivated theoretical framework (evaluability, distinguishing strong vs. weak evaluability, and estimability) that formalizes an important and underexplored question: whether generative model evaluation metrics can actually be compared reliably from finite samples, as opposed to merely being well-defined population quantities.

Provides a comprehensive and largely tight characterization for IPMs: a strict dichotomy between strong evaluability (finite VC dimension) and 3-weak evaluability (unbounded VC dimension) for binary test classes, extending and building on Bousquet et al. (2019) and Yatracos-style density estimation results, with an accompanying fat-shattering-dimension analysis for real-valued test classes.

Delivers striking and non-trivial negative results showing that Renyi/KL divergences and even 'fixed' truncated alternatives like the coverage profile are fundamentally not evaluable from finite samples due to rare-event sensitivity, with rigorous constructive proofs (e.g., Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5) that are intuitive and convincing.

The analysis of perplexity/NLL as a scoring method (Section 5) is directly relevant to practice: it explains, in a principled theoretical way, documented empirical observations that perplexity often fails to track other notions of model quality (TV distance, restricted KL), and identifies the specific geometric mismatch (boundedness/one-sidedness) responsible, along with a positive result under a closeness-in-ratio condition.

The paper is well organized, clearly written, and includes a useful summary table (Table 1) plus an honest and forward-looking discussion of open questions (e.g., non-existence of a finite taxonomy of IPM sample complexities, gap between VC-style dichotomy proofs for binary vs. real-valued test classes, evaluability of estimability itself).

Proofs appear rigorous and are given in detail in the appendix, with careful handling of the various definitions and constructions (e.g., margin assumptions for the coverage profile, ∆-closeness in ratio for TV).
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical illustration or validation, even at a small/toy scale, to connect the abstract results to observed behavior of perplexity, TV, or IPM-based evaluations on real or synthetic generative models; this would substantially strengthen the practical relevance claimed in several places (e.g., 'validating its use in practice').

Several key results remain open/incomplete: the real-valued IPM dichotomy (Proposition 3.4) does not establish optimality of the factor-3 bound (unlike the binary case in Theorem 3.2), and general evaluability of the β-restricted KL divergence beyond the NLL score is left entirely open, leaving the 'nearly complete characterization' claim only partially realized.

The pairwise-comparison definition of evaluability (Definition 2.3), while natural and tractable, is a specific operationalization choice; its relationship to more standard notions like ranking many models or providing absolute confidence intervals is not deeply explored, and it is unclear how sensitive the qualitative conclusions are to this choice.

Positive results such as Proposition 5.6 and Theorem 4.8 rely on fairly strong side conditions (∆-closeness in ratio, margin assumptions) whose plausibility in realistic generative-modeling settings (e.g., large language models with genuinely heavy-tailed token distributions) is asserted rather than empirically or even semi-quantitatively justified.

Some negative results rely on adversarial two/three-point constructions with vanishingly small probability mass; while this is standard practice for such impossibility results and the paper does discuss the underlying intuition, the practical magnitude/frequency of such rare-event pathologies in real-world generative model comparisons is not quantified, which could leave readers uncertain about how often these worst cases bind in practice.

The treatment of X as either finite or general (with different specializations across sections, e.g., discrete constructions for lower bounds vs. general measure-theoretic definitions for divergences) is not always made fully precise, which could cause minor confusion about the exact scope of some theorems.

strengths: The paper introduces a clean and precise formal vocabulary (estimability, weak/strong evaluability) that cleanly separates the question of whether a metric can be estimated in absolute terms from whether it can be used to correctly rank two competing models, which is a genuinely useful conceptual distinction for the generative-model evaluation literature.

The technical results form a fairly comprehensive and internally consistent taxonomy (Table 1), spanning IPMs with binary and real-valued test classes, fixed unbounded tests, Rényi/KL divergences, the coverage profile, and TV/KL as evaluated by perplexity/NLL, giving the paper a systematic feel.

The negative results (Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3, Proposition 4.5) are proven with simple, elegant two/three-point constructions that convincingly illustrate the rare-event pathology underlying non-evaluability of divergence-based metrics, and the paper honestly shows that naive truncation (coverage profile) does not fix the problem.

The analysis of perplexity/NLL as a score function (Section 5) is a nice worked example connecting the abstract framework to a metric of real practical interest, and the margin/closeness-in-ratio conditions needed to rescue evaluability are informative about when perplexity can and cannot be trusted.

The dichotomy for binary IPMs (Theorem 3.2) extending Bousquet et al.'s density-estimation results to the evaluability setting, together with the matching lower bound on the multiplicative factor of 3, is a solid and non-trivial technical contribution.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with zero empirical validation. Given that the central motivating claims (e.g., 'perplexity can remain highly variable and systematically misrepresent the true cross-entropy, even with large datasets') are about real-world evaluation practice, the complete absence of any experiment on real models/text corpora substantially weakens the practical significance of the contribution and makes it hard to gauge how often the pathological constructions in the proofs actually arise in practice.

The framework implicitly assumes an evaluator has oracle access to the exact density q(x) of the models under comparison (required to compute score functions like nll(q, S) or dF(q, q̂)). This is unrealistic for most modern generative models (GANs, diffusion models, black-box samplers) where only samples, not densities, are available, substantially narrowing the applicability of the entire framework to likelihood-based models.

Several of the key building blocks are direct imports from prior work (Yatracos 1985; Bousquet, Kane, Moran 2019; Alon et al. 1997) with the paper's contribution largely being a re-derivation/relabeling of known estimability/approximation results in the new 'evaluability' language (e.g., Theorem 3.2's 3-weak-evaluability essentially restates the Bousquet et al. factor-3 optimality result). This reduces the perceived originality of the strongest results in the paper.

Some positive results rely on assumptions (Δ-closeness in ratio, (N,α)-margin) that are introduced somewhat post hoc specifically to rescue a positive result for a construction that was shown to fail in general, without much justification for why such conditions would hold for practically relevant model pairs, limiting the takeaway value of these theorems.

The real-valued IPM dichotomy (Proposition 3.4) is explicitly incomplete — the authors could not establish that the factor of 3 is tight in this setting, leaving one of the paper's central claimed results as only a partial characterization, which is acknowledged as an open problem rather than resolved.

The evaluation framework (Definition 2.3) is restricted to pairwise comparisons of exactly two candidate models; it's unclear how the framework and its guarantees extend to the practically important setting of ranking many models or providing an absolute score, which is how generative model evaluation is typically used in practice (leaderboards, benchmarks).

The paper builds significantly on a very recent (2025, essentially concurrent) arXiv paper for the coverage profile metric, and the practical motivation for several of the constructed metrics (e.g., β-restricted KL) feels somewhat ad hoc/invented for the purpose of being analyzed rather than metrics that are actually used or advocated for in the community, weakening the significance of results 4.2-5.4.

strengths: Introduces a clean and conceptually useful theoretical framework distinguishing 'estimability' from 'evaluability' (further split into strong vs. c-weak), which formalizes an intuitive but previously informal question: can two generative models be reliably ranked from finite IID samples with respect to a given metric, even if the metric itself cannot be pointwise estimated?

Provides a comprehensive and largely rigorous set of results spanning several important metric families: IPMs (with a clean VC-dimension dichotomy for binary test classes and a fat-shattering-based sufficient condition for real-valued classes), fixed unbounded statistical tests, Rényi/KL divergences, the coverage profile of Chen et al. (2025), and TV distance/restricted KL evaluability via perplexity/nll.

The negative results for Rényi/KL divergences and the coverage profile are supported by clean, interpretable adversarial constructions (rare, undetectable mass swaps) that clarify exactly why these metrics fail, and the paper is honest that these constructions transfer to related divergences (e.g., Hellinger lower bound as a byproduct).

The analysis of perplexity/nll is a nice applied payoff: it formalizes the empirically observed unreliability of perplexity as a model-comparison tool (citing Fang et al. 2025; Hu et al. 2024), identifies precisely when it can/cannot be trusted (∆-closeness-in-ratio assumption for TV, and the impossibility for restricted KL), giving a principled account of a widely used but poorly understood metric.

Theorem 3.6 (no finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs) is an interesting and non-obvious structural result showing that, unlike VC theory for classification, there is no small set of canonical convergence rates governing IPM estimation, which meaningfully extends the standard learning-theory narrative to the evaluation setting.

The paper is transparent about open questions (e.g., tightness of the 3-factor for real-valued IPMs, the general relationship between strong evaluability and estimability, evaluability of restricted KL beyond nll), which is good scientific practice and signals a coherent research program rather than a closed, over-claimed contribution.
weaknesses: The evaluability definition requires correctness uniformly over all pairs (q1, q2) and all ground truths q* in the fully unrestricted model space M = ∆(X); this worst-case framing (essentially minimax over the space of all distributions) is what drives most negative results, and it is not obvious how much of the pessimism (e.g., for Rényi/KL, coverage profile) would persist under realistic structural restrictions on the model class (e.g., parametric neural sequence models), which is a much more relevant setting in practice. This should be discussed more explicitly as a limitation rather than left implicit.

The definition of evaluability is inherently pairwise (comparing exactly two candidate models at a time); the paper does not address whether pairwise-consistent comparisons induced by an evaluation algorithm are transitive across three or more models, which matters if the framework is meant to support model rankings/leaderboards rather than just head-to-head comparisons.

Several of the technical results, while carefully proved, are relatively direct applications/extensions of known PAC-learning and density-estimation machinery (VC dimension, fat-shattering dimension uniform convergence à la Alon et al. 1997/Bartlett et al. 1996, and the 3-factor optimality of Yatracos-type estimators from Bousquet et al. 2019); the core novelty is largely in the reframing (evaluability vs. estimability) and in assembling/extending these tools to new metric families, rather than in fundamentally new proof techniques.

The characterization for real-valued IPMs (Proposition 3.4) is incomplete relative to the binary case: the authors could not establish that the factor-3 bound is tight when the fat-shattering dimension is unbounded, leaving the central dichotomy claimed in the intro only partially proven for this case.

The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical illustration (even small-scale/synthetic) of how these evaluability results manifest in practice — e.g., simulating the perplexity-TV mismatch or the Rényi/KL rare-event failure on toy or real distributions would strengthen the connection between the abstract framework and practical evaluation of generative models.

Some constructions (e.g., in Theorems 4.2, 4.5, 5.3) rely on discrete, small-support toy distributions; while sufficient to prove impossibility, the paper would benefit from discussing whether/how quickly these pathologies emerge in more realistic (e.g., continuous, high-entropy language-model-like) distributions, to help readers calibrate the practical severity of the negative results.
